title: The lawn mower came from a cloth mill
hook: The lawn mower began as a machine for giving woollen cloth a smooth finish.
peek: Edwin Budding worked in Gloucestershire, where cloth mills used spinning blades to shave the fuzz off woollen fabric. In 1830 he patented the same idea on wheels, for cutting grass.
lede: Before 1830, lawns were cut with scythes or kept short by grazing sheep. Edwin Budding, an engineer near Stroud in Gloucestershire, knew the local cloth mills, where a cylinder of spiral blades sheared the raised nap off woollen cloth to leave a smooth finish. He set a similar cylinder between two rollers and pushed it across grass. His patent was granted in 1830.

bullets.text: The mill machine Budding adapted spun a bladed cylinder against a fixed bottom blade, trimming fibres like scissors. His mower worked the same way, which is why most reel mowers today still cut with a scissor action.
Budding went into partnership with John Ferrabee, who owned the Phoenix Iron Works at Thrupp, near Stroud. The early mowers were cast iron, heavy and made in small numbers.
One of the first buyers was the Zoological Gardens in Regent's Park, London. Large estates, sports grounds and colleges followed, as smooth lawns became easier to keep.
Local legend says Budding tested his machine after dark so neighbours would not laugh at him. Historians cannot confirm this, but it is still told around Stroud.
